mappings.note: The diagram hands over 2,8,7, so the graded step is the octet reasoning - one electron short, so it gains one (LO-3, valence electrons and valency) - and then why that leaves a NEGATIVE ion, which is the p-e charge balance from LO-1. Not LO-2: the configuration is given, not built.

POOR FIT and the twin of O11, mapped identically. Absorption on a jump to a higher shell is stated by no outcome; LO-2 is cited only because the answer needs shells to be discrete levels ordered by distance, C1.1 because it is the one intact row naming Bohr's model.
Counting particles off a schematic to get Z = 3 and A = 7 is LO-4, just with the data drawn instead of written. No valency and no element name, so unlike O14 and O21 nothing else is cited.

Fourteen electrons have to be laid out as 2,8,4 (LO-2) and then turned into combining capacity 4 (LO-3, valency). The separation from O14 is that O14 also wants Z and A and so carries LO-4, while this one stops at valency.

The verdict wanted is the word 'isotopes' (LO-3), reached by reading two structural diagrams against each other - LO-5's 'interpret data ... to classify'. Same treatment as the O9 and O16 table items; the only difference here is that the data are drawn.

Distinct from O22 although both are isotope items: O22 asks WHICH relation holds, this asks WHY the chemistry is identical, and the answer is one clause of LO-3 - valence electrons. No LO-5 because nothing is classified; the three species are already given as one element.

POOR FIT, twin of O1 and mapped the same. Acharya Kanada is ancient Indian philosophy, i.e. another curricular area (CG5); C5.1 is the nearest competency but names literature and arts specifically, and its only two outcomes are about drawing diagrams.

POOR FIT. Dalton's theory is not stated anywhere in curriculum 82 - it predates the subatomic particles that LO-1 differentiates, and every other outcome assumes them. CG1 is cited as the goal the content belongs to rather than as an outcome it meets; I would rather record the hole than force LO-1 onto a theory of indivisible atoms.

'What caused scientists to reconsider' is the supersession question in its purest form, so CG7's 'Science is ever evolving' leads. LO-1 follows because what the reconsideration produced is the subatomic particles themselves. Same CG7 rule as P5 and N5: cite it when the revision IS the answer.

A one-sentence description of the plum pudding model is exactly a statement of where the charges sit - a uniform positive sphere with electrons embedded - LO-1's charge and position clauses. Shares its outcome with P2 and O10 honestly; no legal code distinguishes describing the model from critiquing an analogy to it.

POOR FIT, the weakest in the chapter. 'Which material did he use' is apparatus recall: gold foil and an alpha beam. No outcome in curriculum 82 mentions experimental apparatus, and nothing about charge, position, shells, numbers or conventions is graded, so only the goal can be cited.

PARTIAL FIT. This stops at the observation - most through, a few deflected, a very few back - without drawing the conclusion, and observations are not stated by any outcome. LO-1 is one inferential step away and is what the observation exists to establish, so it is the nearest legal code. V30 asks for the conclusion itself and fits LO-1 properly.

This one does draw the structural conclusion - the atom is mostly empty, so its matter sits in a tiny region - which is LO-1's 'position in the atom'. That is the split from V29, which recites the observation and stops.

POOR FIT. The limitation of Rutherford's model is what forced the next model, so CG7 ('Science is ever evolving') is the only text it matches; no outcome states atomic stability or radiation by an accelerating electron. C1.1 is added as the atomic-structure competency. V32, which asks what Bohr's answer was, gets LO-2 instead - the split is defect versus postulate.

PARTIAL FIT. The answer is the stationary-state postulate - fixed orbits where no energy is lost. LO-2 is the only outcome naming energy levels and C1.1 the only intact row naming Bohr's model; the no-energy-loss clause is in neither. Same mapping as N10 for the same reason.

A clean LO-2, unlike its neighbours: the item asks only for the TERM for the fixed paths, and 'energy levels ... such as K, L, M, N' is LO-2's own wording. No C1.1 needed because no postulate of Bohr's model has to be reproduced.

The graded half I can map is the neutron's zero charge, which is LO-1's differentiation by charge. The other half, that Chadwick discovered it in 1932, is covered by nothing in curriculum 82 - the discovery-history gap again.

POOR FIT, and a specific gap worth recording: this item is purely about MASS (neutron about equal to a proton, far heavier than an electron), while LO-1 differentiates the particles by 'charge, and position in the atom' only. The one row that mentions the mass unit alongside the neutron, C-1.3-LO-1, is a stranded fragment with no verb and cannot be cited.

IUPAC is the international body whose standards LO-6 refers to ('use scientific conventions as per international [standards]'), and the answer is that it approves names and symbols. Not C-1.3-LO-2: no element's symbol is recalled or applied.

The capital-then-lower-case rule, which is the convention itself - LO-6. Shares its outcome with P8 honestly: P8 invents a symbol by the rule, this states the rule, and curriculum 82 has no code that separates stating a convention from applying it.

A definition item, and 'atomic number' is named word for word in LO-3's list. Not LO-4: nothing is calculated, and not LO-1, because what is wanted is the definition of the quantity rather than the proton's charge or place.

The relation A = p + n is stated rather than applied, and it is the relation LO-4 is built on ('using its atomic and mass numbers'). LO-3 lists 'atomic mass' but not 'mass number', which are different quantities, so I did not cite it for a mass-number formula.
Defining nucleons is defining two of LO-1's three particles by WHERE they are - packed inside the nucleus. That is the position clause used on its own, with no charge and no counting.

2n-squared is the capacity rule over LO-2's shell numbering (n = 1, 2, 3, 4) and LO-5 names 'maximum number of electrons in a shell' explicitly. Shares this pair with V42 and O5, honestly - one item states the rule, the others apply it, and no legal code separates statement from application.

Same pair as V41 by design: the M shell is n = 3 in LO-2's numbering and 18 is LO-5's 'maximum number of electrons in a shell'. I mapped the two identically rather than invent a distinction between quoting 2n-squared and evaluating it.
